The European greenfinch Chloris chloris is a common passerine across much of Europe and parts of western Asia, and like many cardueline finches, it displays a life history shaped by seasonal resource pulses. The initial weight of the freshly laid egg, representing the very start of embryonic development, has been recorded at 2.17 grams [Ww0 = 2.17 grams], a value that reflects the considerable investment females make into vitellogenesis. This initial mass stands in contrast to the hatchling's mass at emergence from the egg, which is notably lower at 1.6 grams [Wwb = 1.6 grams], a reduction attributable to metabolic consumption of yolk reserves and water loss during the incubation period. The developmental sequence from fertilisation to hatching is completed in approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days] when eggs are incubated steadily at 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. This thermal requirement is typical for finch species, linking the duration of the embryonic period directly to the tight temperature regulation provided by the incubating parent.

Following successful hatching, the altricial nestlings enter a phase of rapid somatic development within the nest. Under the consistently warm conditions that approximate the species' active metabolic body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the young reach the critical milestone of fledging just 13.5 days after hatching [tx = 13.5 days after hatching]. This brief nestling period, culminating in first flight, is a relatively short interval for a finch of its body size and is likely an adaptation to reduce predation risk during the vulnerable early life stages. However, the achievement of permanent flight and nutritional independence does not immediately signal reproductive maturity. Indeed, the onset of puberty, marked by the development of functional gonads and the production of mature gametes, is not reached until approximately 40.5 days after hatching [tp = approximately 40.5 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This gap between fledging and puberty allows young birds to refine their foraging skills and acquire sufficient body condition before the energetic demands of breeding.

The delay between sexual maturation and the actual initiation of reproductive activity is a notable feature of greenfinch life history. Even though puberty is attained by roughly 40 days post-hatching, first-year birds typically defer their first breeding attempt for a considerably longer period. Under a stable thermal environment of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the mean time since birth at the first successful brood is approximately 438 days [tR = approximately 438 days]. This protracted deferral of reproduction into the second calendar year is widespread among cardueline finches and is generally interpreted as a strategy that allows inexperienced individuals to gain vital experience with territory establishment, courtship behaviour, and food resource tracking without the additional physiological stress of egg production and nestling provisioning. The ultimate adult body mass that females achieve after this period of maturation and growth is 28.05 grams [Wwi = 28.05 grams], whereas males, which are typically slightly more streamlined, reach an ultimate wet weight of 27.2 grams [Wwi = 27.2 grams], a modest but consistent sexual size dimorphism.

The reproductive output of the European greenfinch, when assessed under the favourable thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reveals a conservative breeding strategy typical of many temperate-zone finches. Females typically lay a single clutch of between 4 and 6 eggs each year, which equates to an annual output of about 5 eggs per year [Ri = about 5 eggs per year] across a single breeding attempt per season [F_R_i = single breeding attempt per season]. This relatively modest reproductive rate, producing only one brood annually, is constrained by the demands of extended parental care and the seasonal availability of preferred seeds. The longevity of this species, meanwhile, is considerable for a bird of its size. Under the same ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum documented lifespan for individuals in the wild reaches approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years]. This long potential life, amounting to nearly 4,745 days, allows individuals multiple breeding seasons over the course of their lives.

Basal metabolic rate measurements provide insight into the energetic underpinnings of this life-history strategy. In controlled respirometry trials conducted at the species' typical active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the resting oxygen consumption of adult greenfinches was recorded at 85.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 85.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This metabolic rate is characteristic of a bird that balances the energetic costs of thermoregulation with the need to sustain a relatively long lifespan and a modest annual reproductive output. The interplay between this elevated metabolic demand, the 1.6 gram [Wwb = 1.6 gram] hatchling mass, and the protracted period of 438 days [tR = 438 days] before first breeding underscores a life history where investment in somatic longevity and deferred reproduction is prioritised over high immediate fecundity, a strategy that has proven successful across its extensive Palearctic distribution. at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]
